messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Single vs Multi Season
messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily,

I'd second what Jose said.  Season is defined by closure - there should no unaccounted-for changes of occupancy within season; changes of occupancy happen between seasons.  You would need to define closure and season for your study area/species/study design.

-Alex

On Friday, April 29, 2022 at 5:01:08 PM UTC-4 join...@uc.cl wrote:
> Hi Emily,
>
> It depends on your research question(s) and the amount of data. A season is not necessarily a year, it can be another time frame. Multi-season (or dynamic) models are commonly used to estimate colonization and/or extinction probabilities, and to test hypotheses on these parameters (e.g. using covariates). This needs good amounts of data. If you apply a single-season model to 12 months data it seems to me that you will violate the closure assumption. If you don't need to estimate dynamic parameters but you'd like to test for temporal variation in occupancy you could apply a single-season model with random effects (being random effects the camera trap or sampling unit), by stacking months (i.e., your sampling units would be camera-months).
>
> That's my thinking, hope it helps,
>
> Best,

messages.subject_clean: a marketplace for services and coauthorships ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

motivated by a long email that I got asking for stats help I here share an idea that I had had quite a while ago:  Why not using (among many other ways) these Google group help lists as a marketplace for consulting services in exchange for co-authorships ?

Many of us like to render community service by helping others as much as we can. But sometimes this would require too much of a time commitment and so we can’t do this. I have long thought that people could perhaps send out an advertisement of the kind “Stats consulting help wanted: offer co-authorship in exchange”. I have never seen this and I think some people may feel embarrassed to send out such a call for help. But I really don’t see anything illegitimate in this.  Of course, this would not mean that we should stop giving advice or ask for co-authorships unless we work at least a couple hours…

What do others think ?

Thanks and best regards  --- Marc

Dear Mark,

As a person that has benefited over the years several times from information shared in this Google Group (as well as others) (either directly getting responses to my questions or indirectly in reading other people's questiosn being answered), I find your suggestion very logical. I always assumed that people would privately approach more experienced colleagues in data analysis to suggest exactly that - co-authorship in a paper - when more extensive assistance was required (rather than one-time advice on a specific issue), but I guess this is not the norm.

Maybe it would also make sense to have once or twice a year an email sent to all, explaining that such a collaboration (when extensive assistance is saught) is advisable? (this in addition to your suggestion of inviting people to directly post a request for consultanship assistance). I also do not see anything problematic in such an arrangement, as long as all assistance is acknowledged (e.g. in MSc/Phd studies).

I look forward to hearing other members' thoughts.

regards,

Christos

messages.body_plain:
Hi and thank you both for your suggestions!

My research question is to look at site-specific occupancy for gorillas and chimpanzees within a multi-use landscape (19 camera sites over 12 months, with a detection matrix of 52 sampling occasions of one week, although not all sites have 52 sampling occasions). I am doing a separate occupancy model for each species but I will compare them after.

I know there is monthly variation in site occupancy (i.e both species use different sites during different months, although I don't believe either species leaves or enters the study area entirely during the 12 months). Basically I want to be able to determine which sites specifically are used during which months while accounting for imperfect detection. I am also interested in whether certain sites are used by both species during the same time-frame (month, or season) but for now I want to run two separate occupancy models.

The columns of my dataset (I have 1 dataset for each spp) are currently as follows:
site id [1] n=19
site covs  - habitat type (Forest, Road, Trail) , land type (Park, Community, Forestry), # of sampling occasions -  [,2:4]
chimp(or gorilla) detection (y) - [,5:56]
obs covs  - standardized Julian date [,57:108], ecological season (Rainy, Short dry, Short rainy, Dry) [,109:160], month (June2019-May2020) [ ,161:212]

José, you wrote :   "If you don't need to estimate dynamic parameters but you'd like to test for temporal variation in occupancy you could apply a single-season model with random effects (being random effects the camera trap or sampling unit), by stacking months (i.e., your sampling units would be camera-months)."

I believe this is what I want to do, but I'm not sure how to set up my data/unmarked frame.

Instead of my first column being 19 rows of sites, would it be 19*12 rows (i.e  stacked site.month; site1.june, site1.july...site19.may)? Could I then make the ecological season a site cov instead? I'm also missing some data (not all sites have functional cameras for all 12 months). I could stack the site.season, however the ecological seasons (Rainy, Dry, etc) are unequal in length, so it might be problematic.

This is what I have so far for my chimpanzee model (obviously if I switch to the stacked version this would be different):

chimpanzee <- read.csv("chimp.detection.4.csv")

DATE <- as.matrix(chimpanzee[,57:108])    ## Julian date of sampling occasion

y.chimp <- as.matrix(chimpanzee[,5:56])  ##detection matrix

## standardize dates

y.chimp[is.na <http://is.na>(DATE) != is.na <http://is.na>(y.chimp)] <- NA

sd.DATE <- sd(c(DATE), na.rm = TRUE)
mean.DATE <- mean(DATE, na.rm = TRUE)
DATE <- (DATE - mean.DATE) / sd.DATE

# set up site covariates (habitat type, land type, number of sampling occasions)

siteCovs <- chimpanzee[ ,2:4]

# set up obs covariates (season, month)

SEASON <- chimpanzee[,109:160]

MONTH <- chimpanzee[,161:212]

obsCovs <- list(date=DATE, season=SEASON, month= MONTH)

## Now I just need to set up either an unmarkedMultFrame or unmarkedFrameOccu...

Any input would be helpful! I already ran a single-season model which worked fairly well (I think?), but I'm annoyed because I think I must be violating the closure assumption, as I know occupancy varies between the sites each month.

Thank you!
Emily

messages.body_plain:
You should be able to use site covariates in your detection formulas, if you are using the latest version of unmarked. The error you are getting suggests something might be wrong with the way the site covariates were read into R - do you get any errors if you make the detection formulas intercept-only and run the model?

If that isn't working you can also manually turn NDVI into a site covariate by replicating your R NDVI values J times each - i.e., take the NDVI column, copy it J times, and bind the J columns into a new RxJ matrix and supply that as an observation covariate.

Ken

Hi Haqiq,

The approach is
(1) import a raster for each covariate into R using the 'raster' package and raster() function
(2) stack the rasters into a RasterStack using the stack() function, making sure the names of each raster in the stack exactly match the names of your covariates in the model
(3) convert the RasterStack into a data frame using as.data.frame()
(4) use this data frame as the newdata for predict()
(5) Convert the resulting prediction data frame back into a raster of the same extent using rasterFromXYZ()

See this thread, especially the answer from Chris Sutherland, for more details: https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/QTPK3ujKVEc/m/j5x4jRYWJwcJ

Most unmarked functions can do steps 3-5 for you automatically, but unfortunately with occuMulti you have to do them manually.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Dear Sean,

I have three comments:
I think it would be good if you state, perhaps right in the header of the email, whether your question refers to unmarked or ubms. This helps to get into the right "state of mind".
You have extremely sparse information about occurrence. Look at this: there is a sense in which a single-species occupancy model is a combination of two logistic regressions:
one is for the presence/absence of the species at a site, except that you only observe the site occupancy state in an imperfect manner, and have to estimate it
the other is for the actual detection/nondetection measurements, which are actual observed data
Your sample sizes for these two regressions are 22-30 for occupancy and between 500 and 1000 or so for detection. So, you have comparatively plenty of information to learn about the covariates that may affect detection, but you have extremely sparse data to learn about the factors associated with occupancy.

There are various rules of thumb about how many data points you need for each parameter in a regression model and I believe they range between 5 and 20 or so. So in your case, this would mean that you could add perhaps between 1 and 6 covariates into the occupancy model. BUT: you are in a worse position, since you haven't observed the presences and absences, but you must estimate them. So it is not so remarkable perhaps that you would get into problems when you try to estimate more than 1-2 or so covariates in the submodel for p.
But perhaps the most important thing is that a static occupancy model with random site effects is not identifiable. I.e., you can't estimate these parameters. This is related to the usual GLM wisdom (which one can probably find somewhere in the McCullagh and Nelder bible or in some other GLM book) that you can't estimate overdispersion in a binary-response logistic regression.
Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
I think you want projected occupancy, by treatment. If you search the group archives, there are several past discussions of calculating projected occupancy; I think you asked a similar question in the context of unmarked previously?

https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/tn3vqvNOPvI/m/RVMLDqPTCgAJ

You can do something similar with ubms output but it is a bit more complicated because you have the posterior distribution of projected occupancy at each site and primary period, rather than point estimates. Here's a quick example with code and output using the frogs dataset provided with unmarked.

-----------------------------

    set.seed(123)
    suppressMessages(library(ubms))
    data(frogs)
    umf <- formatMult(masspcru)
    umf@y[umf@y>1] <- 1
    obsCovs(umf) <- scale(obsCovs(umf))
    # Make a fake treatment site covariate
    siteCovs(umf) <- data.frame(treat=sample(c("A","B"), numSites(umf), replace=TRUE))

    ## Use 1/4 of data just for run speed in example
    umf <- umf[which((1:numSites(umf)) %% 4 == 0),]

    # Fit in ubms
    # Unsurprisingly treatment coefficient CI overlaps 0 since we made it up
    (mod_stan <- stan_colext(~treat, ~1, ~1, ~JulianDate, umf, chains=3, iter=300, refresh=0))

    ##
    ## Call:
    ## stan_colext(psiformula = ~treat, gammaformula = ~1, epsilonformula = ~1,
    ##     pformula = ~JulianDate, data = umf, chains = 3, iter = 300,
    ##     refresh = 0)
    ##
    ## Occupancy (logit-scale):
    ##             Estimate    SD   2.5% 97.5% n_eff  Rhat
    ## (Intercept)   1.4028 0.422  0.638  2.31   358 0.994
    ## treatB       -0.0321 0.598 -1.322  1.25   359 0.998
    ##
    ## Colonization (logit-scale):
    ##  Estimate    SD  2.5%  97.5% n_eff Rhat
    ##     -1.23 0.466 -2.19 -0.389   370    1
    ##
    ## Extinction (logit-scale):
    ##  Estimate    SD  2.5% 97.5% n_eff  Rhat
    ##     -2.91 0.429 -3.85 -2.15   390 0.999
    ##
    ## Detection (logit-scale):
    ##             Estimate    SD   2.5%   97.5% n_eff Rhat
    ## (Intercept)   -0.133 0.111 -0.339  0.0858   432    1
    ## JulianDate    -2.108 0.154 -2.407 -1.8230   391    1
    ##
    ## LOOIC: 716.484
    ## Runtime: 5.508 sec

    # Get projected occupancy at each site and primary period

    # Dimensions: nsamples x (# sites x # primary periods in site-major order)
    # see ?ubms::projected
    proj_occ <- projected(mod_stan)

    # Re-arrange into array samples x primary period x nsite
    proj_occ <- array(proj_occ, c(nsamples(mod_stan), umf@numPrimary, numSites(umf)))

    # Calculate mean occupancy across sites in each sample and primary period
    # This ignores treatment for now
    proj_mean <- apply(proj_occ, c(1,2), mean)

    # Summarize across samples to get mean occupancy per primary period
    colMeans(proj_mean)

    ## [1] 0.7913132 0.7964553 0.7993061 0.8008328 0.8015986 0.8019320 0.8020245

    # Now get estimates by treatment using the proj_occ array

    # Instead of calculating overall mean, calculate mean for each treatment
    mean_by_treat <- function(x){
      treat <- siteCovs(umf)$treat
      c(treatA = mean(x[treat == "A"]),
        treatB = mean(x[treat == "B"]))
    }

    # Apply over each sample and primary period
    proj_treat <- apply(proj_occ, c(1,2), mean_by_treat)

    # Calculate mean estimate across all samples
    treatment_est <- apply(proj_treat, c(1,3), mean)

    # 95% CI
    lower <- apply(proj_treat, c(1,3), quantile, 0.025)
    upper <- apply(proj_treat, c(1,3), quantile, 0.975)

    # Build plot
    plot(1:7-0.1, treatment_est[1,], ylim=c(0.5, 1), type='o', col='blue',
        ylab="Occupancy and 95% CI", xlab="Primary period")
    segments(1:7-0.1, lower[1,], 1:7-0.1, upper[1,], col='blue')
    lines(1:7+0.1, treatment_est[2,], type='o', col='red')
    segments(1:7+0.1, lower[2,], 1:7+0.1, upper[2,], col='red')
    legend('bottomright', lty=1, col=c("blue","red"), legend=c("A","B"),
            title="Treatment")

On Friday, May 20, 2022 at 9:43:52 AM UTC-4 Kery Marc wrote:
> Dear Sean,
>
> I have three comments:
> I think it would be good if you state, perhaps right in the header of the email, whether your question refers to unmarked or ubms. This helps to get into the right "state of mind".
> You have extremely sparse information about occurrence. Look at this: there is a sense in which a single-species occupancy model is a combination of two logistic regressions:
> one is for the presence/absence of the species at a site, except that you only observe the site occupancy state in an imperfect manner, and have to estimate it
> the other is for the actual detection/nondetection measurements, which are actual observed data
> Your sample sizes for these two regressions are 22-30 for occupancy and between 500 and 1000 or so for detection. So, you have comparatively plenty of information to learn about the covariates that may affect detection, but you have extremely sparse data to learn about the factors associated with occupancy.
>
> There are various rules of thumb about how many data points you need for each parameter in a regression model and I believe they range between 5 and 20 or so. So in your case, this would mean that you could add perhaps between 1 and 6 covariates into the occupancy model. BUT: you are in a worse position, since you haven't observed the presences and absences, but you must estimate them. So it is not so remarkable perhaps that you would get into problems when you try to estimate more than 1-2 or so covariates in the submodel for p.
> But perhaps the most important thing is that a static occupancy model with random site effects is not identifiable. I.e., you can't estimate these parameters. This is related to the usual GLM wisdom (which one can probably find somewhere in the McCullagh and Nelder bible or in some other GLM book) that you can't estimate overdispersion in a binary-response logistic regression.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily,

unmarked uses the Armadillo C++ library for linear algebra via RcppArmadillo. It seems that when you have very large datasets (and thus large model matrices etc.), Armadillo or perhaps one of its underlying libraries automatically does some computations in parallel if you have openMP support on your computer. I have also noticed this for occuMulti. So far I have not found a way to disable this from inside or outside R, despite trying setting various environmental variables, so I am not sure if there is much we can do about it at this point short of not using RcppArmadillo. If anyone on the list has figured out how to change this I would be very interested.

You're correct that the threads argument in occu() doesn't do anything at the moment. I was planning to add some parallel computation functionality to occu at some point, but didn't (partially because of the issue you have), so the argument needs to be removed. It does currently work on some other functions as you noted such as occuRN.

Can you try running the model with engine="TMB" assuming you are on an up-to-date unmarked? The TMB engine should be similarly fast but uses RcppEigen instead of RcppArmadillo, and based on my tests, does not seem to try to use more than one thread.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I searched the group for an answer but didn’t came up with a solution to my problem. I am currently working on line transect distance sampling data of reptiles (lizards), acquired with a double independent observer sampling protocol, in order to correct for p < 1 on the transect line at perpendicular d = 0 (perception bias). The sampling protocol is quite simple and generates MRDS data:

-       On the field two observers walk simultaneously across the transect line and independently spots lizards.

-       Observers instantly reconcile encounter histories and partition observation in three categories: 1- lizard detected only by obs A, 2 – lizard detected only by obs B, 3 – lizard detected by both obs A and B.

-       For each observation, perpendicular distance from the transect line is recorded.

Data obtained with this protocol can be analysed as double observer DS data with package mrds, or with unmarked function “gdistsamp”, treating independent observations of the two observers as primary sampling periods. However, since also an “availability” bias is possible (lizard activity varies over the season or between different days), I’m interested in estimating the availability by visiting the same transect (or a subset of them) on different days across the season. I’ve read on previous topics of the group that “gdistsamp” cannot handle multiple secondary surveys within a primary period, is that right? Is there any other way or workaround in unmarked to analyse this kind of data, combining DS with Double Ovserver, obtaining both an estimate of perception and availability?

I know that this is doable in Bugs/Jags, but my first choice would be to use Unmarked.

I hope this discussion will also be helpful for others working on similar data…

Thanks to everyone who maintain the package,

Andrea
